title: Synara turns installed security cameras into an ongoing monitoring service
summary: Synara turns installed security cameras into an ongoing monitoring service
body_markdown:
Installing a security camera is a one-time project. Watching it every night is an ongoing service.[Synara](https://synaraops.com/) is building its business around that distinction, offering AI-assisted remote monitoring that security integrators can sell under their own names.


The company launched on October 20 with a promise to do more than detect something unusual on a feed. Its service is intended to verify events, intervene through live audio and escalate a confirmed incident when needed. It connects to existing cameras and recording systems, so a customer doesn't have to replace hardware simply to add monitoring.


Despite the AI emphasis, Synara's public website describes a combined software-and-operator workflow. Detection models triage activity; trained people verify events and decide when to speak to someone on site or request a response. That human role is important to understanding the service being offered.


[Watch Synara's launch video.](https://youtu.be/CYWByOxw344)


The product covers familiar perimeter monitoring tasks, including people or vehicles entering an area, loitering and crossing a boundary. Synara also describes identifying incidents such as falls and collisions, then preserving timestamped clips and reports. Those records are intended to help site operators understand what happened and document the event afterward.


Construction yards, dealerships and warehouses are among the uses the company highlights. They share a practical problem: cameras can record activity at times when nobody is physically available to watch them. A monitoring service must distinguish an event worth escalating from routine movement, then connect the alert to a useful response.


The business model is aimed at the integrator rather than only the property owner. Synara says partners can put their own branding on the portal, reports and invoices, retain the customer relationship and bill monthly. The installed camera base becomes the starting point for a recurring service instead of the end of a hardware project.


Founder Boris Ploix's company is part of Y Combinator's Fall 2026 batch. Its launch describes same-day setup without new hardware, while the website lists compatibility with existing network video recorders and video management systems. Actual setup requirements will depend on the equipment and access available at a site.


Synara advertises around-the-clock coverage and rapid intervention. The announcement does not establish independently measured detection accuracy or response times across customer sites. Its website also labels its example incidents and some footage as illustrative or AI-generated, so those scenes should not be mistaken for records of real events the service handled.


The operational promise is narrower and more useful than an all-seeing camera: filter a feed, have someone verify the important event, and take the next step. For an installer deciding whether to add monitoring to its offering, the question is whether Synara can deliver that sequence consistently while leaving the customer relationship in the installer's hands.
